entries.topic: Poverty line: Orshansky, SPM, ALICE, guidelines, full-income critique

claims.text: Mollie Orshansky of the Social Security Administration developed the thresholds in 1963-64 (published January 1965 Social Security Bulletin), from the USDA economy food plan, which USDA described as 'designed for temporary or emergency use when funds are low'; multiplier 3 for families of 3+ (3.7 for two-person), from the 1955 Household Food Consumption Survey (food about one-third of after-tax income); OEO adopted May 1965; Bureau of the Budget made them the official statistical definition August 1969 and switched indexing to the CPI; 1981 removed farm and sex-of-head distinctions (124 to 48 thresholds); NAS panel May 1995 'Measuring Poverty: A New Approach'

P60-290: official measure thresholds are 'Three times the cost of a minimum food diet in 1963'; SPM 13.1% in 2025, 2.9 points above the official+ rate of 10.2%; not statistically different from 2024; SPM children 13.4%, 65+ 15.4%; Social Security lifted 28.8m out of SPM poverty (-8.5 points); refundable tax credits 6.1m incl. 3.3m children (-1.8 points); medical expenses pushed 7.7m into poverty (+2.3 points); median work expenses $42/week; SPM thresholds set at 82% of median spending on food, clothing, shelter, utilities, telephone, internet, 5-year average of CE data, adjusted for housing tenure and local housing costs; Figure 4 labels 2009 SPM 15.1, official+ 14.4; all SPM estimates 2019-2024 use revised BLS thresholds of 17 July 2026
P60-283 figure: SPM 2023 12.9%, official 2023 11.1%; 2009 SPM 15.1%, official 14.4% (labels)

Census correction: errors in imputations of in-kind benefits in SPM thresholds; corrected 2019-2023 rates 0.1-0.3 points lower than first published; 2024 marginally higher at 12.9-13.0%; thresholds rebased to 82% of median expenditures from 83%

Census: official measure 'remained mostly unchanged since it was introduced in the mid-1960s'; updated by CPI-U; gross pre-tax cash income; ignores in-kind benefits, tax credits and regional cost differences; SPM developed after 2010 interagency working group drawing on the 1995 NAS report; National Academies April 2023 report 'An Updated Measure of Poverty: (Re)Drawing the Line'

ALICE (Asset Limited, Income Constrained, Employed), 2024 data: 131,939,401 households; 16,495,052 (13%) below the Federal Poverty Level; 38,027,832 (29%) ALICE; 54,522,884 (41%) below the ALICE Threshold; Household Survival Budget costs housing, child care, food, transportation, health care, technology for every county
HHS 2026 poverty guidelines, 48 contiguous states: 1 person $15,960; 2 $21,640; 3 $27,320; 4 $33,000

Burkhauser et al.: official poverty 19.5% (1963) to 10.5% (2019); absolute full-income poverty 19.5% to 1.6% (2019); relative full-income poverty 19.5% to 16.0%; attribute to doubled real median income and transfers/tax benefits not counted officially

entries.topic: Criminal-legal costs: incarceration, bail, fines and fees, phones, commissary, labour, records, child support

claims.text: Commercial bail: nonrefundable premium usually about 10% of the bond, collateral; about $2bn a year in premiums; sureties paid less than 1% in bail losses (Mother Jones review of 32 sureties); only the US and the Philippines have commercial bail; uncollected forfeitures e.g. Dallas County at least $35m

Illinois ended cash bail 18 September 2023 (Pretrial Fairness Act); Loyola first-year review: jail populations down about 14% (Cook and collar counties) and 25% (rural); failure to appear 22.8% vs 25.1% (21 counties); reported crime down 11% H1 2024 vs H1 2023, with authors noting crime fell everywhere

Bearden v. Georgia (24 May 1983, O'Connor): court may not revoke probation for nonpayment without inquiring into the reasons; if the person cannot pay despite bona fide efforts, alternatives must be considered; 'it is fundamentally unfair to revoke probation automatically'

DOJ Ferguson findings: fines and fees about 13% of the municipal budget 2012, budgeted 23% FY2015; 90,000 citations and summonses 2010-2014 in a city of 21,000; City Manager: the City cannot afford 'any decrease in our Fines and Forfeitures'
California AB 1869 (2020) repealed 23 criminal administrative fees effective 1 July 2021, with $65m to backfill counties

FCC adopted the 2024 IPCS order in July 2024 under the Martha Wright-Reed Act, lowering per-minute caps, capping video, banning site commissions; on 30 June 2025 the Wireline Competition Bureau waived compliance deadlines from 1 April 2026 to 1 April 2027

Oct 2025 FCC order raised interim audio caps per minute: prisons $0.06 to $0.11; large jails $0.06 to $0.10; medium $0.07 to $0.12; small $0.09 to $0.13; very small $0.12 to $0.15; extremely small $0.19; video prisons $0.16 to $0.25; site-commission ban retained; safety and security costs included in caps

FCC DA 26-319 (3 April 2026): 2025 IPCS Order FCC 25-75 adopted 28 October 2025, published 5 December 2025, compliance date 6 April 2026; Securus granted waiver for video per-minute pricing to 6 July 2026

PPI commissary (May 2018): average annual commissary spending $1,121 (IL), $1,207 (MA), $513 (WA), three-state average $947; typical prison job pays $180-$660 a year; a $1.87 pack of floss takes over 13 hours of work at 14 cents an hour in Massachusetts

ACLU/GHRC Captive Labor (15 June 2022): about 800,000 incarcerated workers (65%); at least $2bn goods and $9bn prison maintenance services a year; average non-industry wages 15 to 52 cents an hour; Alabama, Arkansas, Florida, Georgia, Mississippi, South Carolina, Texas pay nothing for most jobs; over 80% do maintenance; up to 80% of pay withheld; 20 states have similar constitutional exception clauses

Brennan Center (15 Sept 2020): imprisonment reduces annual earnings by up to 51.7%; lifetime losses after imprisonment as a young adult $267,000 (white), $358,900 (Black), $511,500 (Latino); aggregate $372.3bn a year for people with a conviction or prison time ($55.2bn for formerly imprisoned); at least 7m have been in prison; 45m have a misdemeanor conviction, losing 16% of annual earnings
Pager Milwaukee audit: callbacks white no record 34%, white with record 17%, Black no record 14%, Black with record 5%

Agan and Starr: about 15,000 applications in NYC and NJ; applicants without records got 63% more callbacks; white-Black callback gap about 7% before Ban the Box, 45% after among affected employers; mechanism: statistical discrimination

ASPE July 2020: about 20% of inmates have child support orders; average parent enters prison with about $10,000 in arrears and leaves with about $20,000 (NCSL 2019); as of July 2019 at least 9 states/territories treated incarceration as voluntary unemployment; the 2016 modernization rule prohibits that

entries.topic: Homelessness: HUD 2025 count, Grants Pass, 2025 executive order, CoC litigation, Housing First evidence

claims.text: HUD (29 May 2026): Jan 2025 PIT 745,652 homeless, 266,320 unsheltered, down 3% from 2024, up 27% since 2013; unsheltered up 36% and chronic up 81% since 2013; release attributes decline to 'decreases in Sanctuary Cities'; Turner: 'the status quo of housing first has failed to meaningfully reduce homelessness'; 2013-2025 taxpayer-funded beds up 151%, CoC spending up 111%; 1,456,923 homeless or in homeless-funded housing

Grants Pass v. Johnson (28 June 2024, 6-3, Gorsuch): Eighth Amendment does not bar enforcement of general public-camping laws; Grants Pass ordinance: civil fines, then bans and short jail terms for repeat violations; Gorsuch: 'Homelessness is complex. Its causes are many.'; Sotomayor dissent (Kagan, Jackson): 'unconscionable and unconstitutional'

EO 'Ending Crime and Disorder on America's Streets' (24 July 2025): ends federal support for Housing First, prioritises treatment, HUD to condition participation on treatment; promotes civil commitment; SAMHSA not to fund harm reduction or safe consumption; grants to favour jurisdictions that enforce bans on open drug use, urban camping, loitering, squatting

FY2025 CoC NOFO (13 Nov 2025) capped permanent supportive housing at 30% (PSH about 87% of CoC spending) and tier 1 at 30% (from about 90%); sued by 21 state AGs and local governments; HUD withdrew it 8 Dec 2025; under injunction restored prior-year competition; Consolidated Appropriations Act 2026 (3 Feb 2026, sec. 244) directed renewals of expiring projects

CRS 18 Sept 2026: FY2026 CoC NOFO released 1 June 2026, modified 24 July 2026; tier 1 60% of annual renewal demand; $1.3bn of $4.04bn set aside for new transitional housing and supportive-services-only projects; points for treatment and recovery and for requiring participation in services; court vacated NOFO 7 Aug 2026 under APA; HUD appealed 13 Aug; First Circuit panel stayed vacatur 16 Sept 2026

NACo: case National Alliance to End Homelessness v. HUD; court found the $1.3bn set-aside and criteria requiring adherence to executive orders unlawful; after the 16 Sept stay HUD reinstated the NOFO with a 30 Sept 2026 deadline

J-PAL review: At Home/Chez Soi Housing First participants stably housed 73% of two years vs 32%; HUD-VASH housed in 35 vs 223 days; health effects unclear; substance-use outcomes similar to treatment-first; cost largely offset by savings, evidence limited

NASEM 2018: 'the committee found no substantial evidence that PSH contributes to improved health outcomes' (limited data for HIV/AIDS); 'PSH increases an individual's ability to remain housed'; more cost-effectiveness research needed

Colburn and Aldern (2022): mental illness, drug use, poverty, weather, generosity of assistance do not explain regional variation in homelessness; housing market conditions, such as the cost and availability of rental housing, offer a far more convincing account

claims.text: Loyola first-year review (21 counties): failure to appear for non-detainable felonies rose from 28.1% to 31%; overall fell 25.1% to 22.8%; authors called FTA changes 'minimal'; violent crime -7%, property -14% (H1 2024 vs H1 2023); share still held three days after arrest fell from 33% to 9%
